page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — closing paragraph beginning 'The architect's verdict:'
quoted_clause: Until it does, start on the managed API now (conditional on the startup's $26K/mo 0.5 FTE engineer staffing basis) as the default while that opportunity cost is unmeasured, and revisit self-host the moment it is measured below ~$90K/month
observed: The mini-case's final recommendation (start on the API) is not derived from its own analysis, which yields self-host unless the freed 0.5 FTE is worth more than ~$90K/mo. The prose never states the expected-value argument that would justify departing from the modeled answer, so the recommendation reads as a contradiction of the preceding paragraphs.
evidence: The modeled answer with V = 0 (no alternative product value for the freed hours) is self-host with a $64K/mo saving. The threshold of $90.2K/mo corresponds to $1.08M/yr of product output for a 0.5 FTE, i.e. ~$2.16M/yr per FTE — a bar that the mini-case's own framing ('about $1.08M/year of product work the startup is not doing') makes look implausible for a startup. The chapter also states earlier in the same mini-case: 'The token arithmetic alone therefore does not send this startup to the API; it points to self-hosting.' The recommendation is therefore a risk/reversibility choice, not an analytical conclusion, and is not labelled as such.
root_cause: The mini-case ends with a decision that its model does not produce; the gap between 'the model says self-host unless V > $90K' and 'default to the API' is left implicit rather than argued.
correction: Either (a) state the recommendation as an explicit risk-aversion/reversibility choice with its cost ('starting on the API forgoes ~$64K/mo of modeled saving and is reversible; buying the servers is not'), or (b) change the default to self-host with the threshold stated as the check to run, noting that the threshold is high enough that self-host is the expected outcome unless the engineer is unusually valuable. Whichever is chosen, label the recommendation as a decision under an unmeasured input rather than as the model's conclusion.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's final recommendation must be traceable to a stated argument (expected value or reversibility), and must not read as the output of the break-even arithmetic it follows.

page_hint: Ch 15 §8 mini-case — MFU sentence beginning 'The MFU stabilizes at ~62 %…'
quoted_clause: against the two-host 15.82 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s peak (half of the ~124 % one-host figure in §6)
observed: The parenthetical is not self-explanatory and appears to import a >100% utilization figure from §6. If §6 presents '~124%' as an MFU or utilization percentage, it exceeds 100% and contradicts Ch 8's MFU definition; if it is a token rate, the percentage and the rate are being conflated in one phrase.
evidence: The only clean numerical fit for '124%' in this chapter is 70,000 tok/s ÷ 56,500 tok/s = 1.239 — i.e. §6's one-host figure appears to be a 70,000 tok/s rate expressed as a percentage of the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling. A single host cannot exceed its own 100%-MFU ceiling, so such a figure is either a ceiling (not a measurement) or an error. The mini-case's own arithmetic is sound: 70,000 × 140e9 = 9.8e15 FLOP/s against 16 × 989e12 = 15.82e15 → 61.9% ≈ 62%, and 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 56,500 = 62%. The problem is the cross-reference, not the MFU.
root_cause: The parenthetical was written as a shorthand link to a §6 figure whose quantity and denominator are not restated, and the §6 figure itself has not been checked against the MFU definition.
correction: Restate the parenthetical with quantity and denominator, e.g. 'the two-host aggregate equals the single-host rate quoted in §6, i.e. 35,000 tok/s per host = 62% of the 56,500 tok/s 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling'. Then audit §6: if it states a one-host rate of ~70,000 tok/s, it must be labelled a ceiling or an upper bound, not a measured rate, and any '124%' must be explicitly framed as 'above the 100%-MFU ceiling, therefore not achievable' rather than as a utilization figure.
acceptance_test: No figure in Ch 15 or Ch 16 may be presented as an MFU/utilization percentage above 100%; the parenthetical must name the quantity and its denominator; §6's one-host figure must be checked and, if it is a ceiling, labelled as such.

page_hint: Ch 16 §2 (Mental Model), second bullet
quoted_clause: Two systems with the same card count can differ 10× in cost per request when 3× the goodput per card composes with ~3.4× from better utilization and no idle coasting.
observed: The decomposition double-counts utilization: goodput per card already contains utilization (goodput/card = capacity/card × utilization × SLO-pass rate), so '3× the goodput per card' and '3.4× from better utilization' cannot be independent multiplicative factors. The arithmetic (3 × 3.4 ≈ 10) works, but the model behind it does not.
evidence: The chapter's own §16.4 defines 'Raw utilization = served ÷ provisioned; effective utilization = SLO-meeting goodput ÷ theoretical capacity', and §16.3's fleet sizing uses utilization as a derate on slot occupancy and scheduling efficiency. Under those definitions, a 3× goodput-per-card improvement already includes whatever utilization change produced it; multiplying by a further 3.4× utilization factor double-counts the same physical resource.
root_cause: The bullet was written as an illustrative magnitude ('10×') and the factors were chosen to reach it, rather than being derived from a decomposition the chapter defines elsewhere.
correction: Rewrite the bullet with a decomposition consistent with §16.4, e.g. 'Two systems with the same card count can differ 10× in cost per request: 3× from higher per-card capacity (better kernels, better quantization) × 3.4× from higher effective utilization (better batching, higher SLO-goodput per slot) — the two are independent levers, and the second is the one most often left on the table.'
acceptance_test: The factors named in the bullet must map one-to-one onto the chapter's own definitions of capacity and utilization, with no quantity appearing in both factors.

page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — 'The honest number:' paragraph and the 'On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc' sentence
quoted_clause: capex ~$11.6K + power ~$2.2K for two hosts leaves ≤ ~$26K for staff ... self-host = 13.8 + 6.5 = $20.3K/mo ... On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc the self-host cost is ~$23.8K/mo

page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (Measurement, 'Which one drives KV residency?') vs §8 (Mini-Case, 'Initial sizing analysis' and 'Decision')
quoted_clause: §4: "Do not substitute a p95/p99 for E[W] in Little's Law. Little's Law is a *mean* relation, E[L] = λ·E[W]; pairing a mean λ with a p95 W mixes moments and yields a number that is neither a mean population nor a percentile one."  §8: "At T = 3 (the 95th-percentile, and the honest stress-cohort sizing point — 'worst case' applies only to the 2% fallback route, F-01) ... N ≈ ⌈1,770/(13 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,770/8.645⌉ ≈ **205 working hosts**" and "the integer-slot FP8 bound under **no-reuse** is **99 working hosts at the 70% × 95% policy, plus one spare host for N−1 operation: 100 hosts in total**"
observed: The chapter states a hard rule (percentile W must not be substituted into the mean Little's Law identity) and then bases its entire mini-case decision on the 95th-percentile turn count T=3, with no mean-based fleet count anywhere in the chapter. The chapter's own F-01 box supplies the distribution-weighted mean W ≈ 12.71 s but never converts it into a host count, so the reader is left with a single (stress-cohort) number presented as 'the Decision'.
evidence: Recomputation from the chapter's own inputs: distribution 0.68/0.25/0.05/0.02 over T=1/2/3/fallback; I(1)=10,365, I(2)=11,230, I(3)=12,095, I(fallback)=9,500 tokens; κ=2.62144 MB/token → per-request KV 27.171 / 29.438 / 31.705 / 24.904 GB; distribution-weighted mean bytes ≈ 0.68(27.171)+0.25(29.438)+0.05(31.705)+0.02(24.904) ≈ 27.92 GB → C = 436/27.92 ≈ 15.6 → floor 15. With F-01's mean W ≈ 12.71 s at 100 rps: in-flight ≈ 1,271 → N = ⌈1,271/(15×0.70×0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,271/9.975⌉ = ⌈127.4⌉ ≈ 128 working hosts (FP16) — versus the 205 the chapter reports for the same traffic point. The stress-cohort figure is ~1.6× the mean-based figure. (The mean-based number is itself approximate because E[bytes×time] ≠ E[bytes]·E[time], which the chapter itself notes.)
root_cause: The chapter separates 'mean' and 'stress cohort' ledgers in F-01 but never propagates the mean ledger into the sizing output; the mini-case's decision line inherits the stress cohort without qualification.
correction: Add the distribution-weighted mean case as a first-class row of Table 17-2 (or a second mini-case column): mean W ≈ 12.71 s, mean per-request KV ≈ 27.9 GB, C ≈ 15 (floor), and the resulting N at 40/100/200 rps. Then state explicitly which number is the planning decision (e.g. 'size to the mean, hold the stress cohort as the tail-risk bound') and label the T=3 columns as the stress bound they are. Reconcile the §4 rule with the §8 practice by pointing at the new mean row rather than at F-01's caveat.
acceptance_test: Table 17-2 contains a distribution-weighted-mean row whose N values are reproducible from F-01's mean W and the distribution-weighted mean bytes; the mini-case's 'Decision' paragraph names which row is the decision and which is the bound; no sentence in Ch 17 pairs a percentile W with a mean Little's Law identity without an explicit stress-cohort label.

page_hint: Ch 17 §4 ('The KV population is its own derivation' paragraph)
quoted_clause: "then adjusted for the **rank/replication layout** (tensor-parallel rank count, and whether KV is sharded across ranks or replicated) and the **admission policy** (whole-context admission with no fractional slots; a prefix-cache hit or a pre-reserved block changes the effective holding time, not the byte geometry)."
observed: The claim that a prefix-cache hit changes 'the effective holding time, not the byte geometry' is incorrect for the mechanism the chapter elsewhere relies on. When a prefix is shared across requests, the marginal KV bytes attributable to a new request are the *delta* (the newly appended tokens), not the whole context; the cached prefix is resident once and reused. The chapter's own reuse scenario (§8, W=14.16 s) is built on exactly this mechanism, so the statement contradicts the chapter's use of prefix caching.
evidence: In §8's reuse case the prefill of the final call is 11,795 tokens of which 9,200 are the cached prefix; the KV for those 9,200 tokens is resident once per shared prefix, not once per request. The chapter nevertheless keeps C = 13 (full 12,095-token context) for the reuse rows of Table 17-2, i.e. it charges every request for the whole context while simultaneously claiming the prefix is shared. The two statements cannot both be true; the reuse rows are conservative in bytes but the accompanying mechanism claim is wrong.
root_cause: The 'byte geometry' sentence was written to prevent a specific transplant error (queue time into KV slots) and over-generalized into a claim about prefix caching, which is a different mechanism.
correction: Split the sentence: (a) a pre-reserved block changes the *holding time* (and can change the admission granularity), not the per-request byte geometry; (b) a prefix-cache hit changes *both* — the marginal bytes per request (delta-only) and the effective holding time — and its capacity benefit depends on the prefix-hit rate and on whether the cached prefix is shared across concurrent requests or pinned to one. Then state which assumption the reuse rows of Table 17-2 use (full-context C, i.e. no byte credit for prefix sharing) and label it as conservative.
acceptance_test: The chapter contains no sentence asserting that prefix caching leaves byte geometry unchanged; Table 17-2's reuse rows state explicitly whether any byte credit is taken for shared prefixes, and the §8 reuse narrative is consistent with that statement.

page_hint: Ch 17 §4 ('Effect on the headline counts')
quoted_clause: "Under case (i) the available headroom is only ~7%; under cases (ii) and (iii) the prefill leg alone exceeds the idealized ceiling, so headroom is negative — the real headroom is smaller than ~7% and may be negative."  vs  "the check pushes the real count upward — by at least the ~7% headroom deficit under case (i), and by more than that under cases (ii)/(iii), where the prefill leg already exceeds the ceiling."

Under case (i) the prefill leg consumes 93% of the ceiling, so the deficit is negative (there is 7% of headroom, not a 7% shortfall). The second sentence then uses the deficit to claim the host count must be pushed upward by 'at least ~7%', which does not follow from a positive 7% headroom.
evidence: 18,400 ÷ 19,780 = 0.9302 → headroom 6.98%. A 7% headroom means the prefill leg could grow by 7% before the ceiling binds; it does not imply a 7% capacity shortfall. The upward push under case (i) is already captured by the policy screens reported elsewhere in the chapter (⌈18.60/0.665⌉+1 = 29 for case (i), versus 32 for the KV-only policy total), so the paragraph double-counts the effect it claims to add.
root_cause: The paragraph was written as a 'the check pushes the count up' narrative and reuses the 7% figure with the wrong sign, without reconciling against the policy-level prefill screens already tabulated in Table 17-1's caption and Table 17-2's note.
correction: Rewrite the paragraph to state the sign correctly: under case (i) the prefill leg leaves ~7% headroom at full utilization, so the prefill screen (18.60 hosts) does not bind against the KV screen (21 hosts); under cases (ii)/(iii) it binds. Then point to the already-reported policy-level screens (29 / 32 / 34) as the place where the prefill constraint enters the host count, instead of asserting an additional upward push.
acceptance_test: The word 'deficit' is not applied to the case-(i) 7% figure anywhere in Ch 17; the 'Effect on the headline counts' paragraph cites the same 29/32/34 policy screens as Table 17-1 and Table 17-2 rather than introducing a separate, unsourced increment.
